title: Design a Logging Framework: Logger, LogLevel (DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR), Appender (console/file/remote), Formatter, singleton logger, thread safety.
topicTitle: LLD Problems: Parking Lot, Elevator, Chess, etc.
keyPoints: The Logger checks a minimum LogLevel threshold and discards messages below it cheaply.
Levels are ordered DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR; the threshold filters what passes through.
An Appender interface abstracts the destination: ConsoleAppender, FileAppender, RemoteAppender (Strategy pattern).
A Formatter turns a level, timestamp, and message into a formatted line, pluggable independently of the appender.
Messages are passed as supplier lambdas so string building is deferred until the level is confirmed enabled.
Thread safety is non-negotiable: appenders must synchronise writes or use a lock-free queue for concurrent logging.
In high-throughput banking systems, an asynchronous appender backed by a ring buffer keeps logging from blocking the business thread.

s1_definition.oneliner: A logging framework filters by level, formats the message, and fans it out to multiple appenders, safely across threads.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Logger** – holds a minimum `LogLevel` threshold; discards messages below the threshold cheaply.
- **LogLevel** – ordered enum: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR.
- **Appender** – interface abstracting the destination (console, file, remote); a Strategy for where logs go.
- **Formatter** – turns a level, timestamp, and message into a formatted output line.
- **LoggerFactory** – hands out loggers, typically cached per name as a Singleton.
- **Thread safety** – appenders must synchronise writes or use a lock-free queue for concurrent logging.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the logging framework as the audit department at National Bank of India. Every action Rajesh takes is reported. The department decides which reports are important enough to keep (level threshold), stamps each with a standard header (formatter), and files copies to several places: a local binder, a central archive, and a monitoring desk (appenders). Many tellers report at once, so the filing must be orderly and safe (thread safety).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Logging Pipeline:
  ─────────────────

  logger.info(() -> "message")
       │
       ▼
  Level check: INFO >= threshold?
       │
       ├── no → discard (cheap, no string built)
       │
       └── yes → build string from supplier
                    │
                    ▼
              Formatter.format(level, name, message)
                    │
                    ▼
              ┌─────┴──────────────┐
              ▼                    ▼
        ConsoleAppender     FileAppender
        (synchronized)      (synchronized)
```

```text
  Logger
    │
    ├── threshold: INFO
    ├── formatter: SimpleFormatter
    └── appenders:
         ├── ConsoleAppender
         ├── FileAppender (/var/log/bank.log)
         └── AsyncAppender → RemoteAppender (Kafka)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When you design a logging framework, separate four responsibilities so each can evolve independently. The Logger decides whether a message passes the configured level threshold. The Formatter decides how a line looks. The Appender decides where it goes. And a LoggerFactory hands out loggers that share configuration. This separation is what lets a framework support console in development and file plus remote in production without rewriting the core.

Levels are ordered from debug up to error, and the Logger holds a minimum threshold so anything below it is discarded cheaply. A key efficiency trick is accepting the message as a supplier lambda, so the string is only built when the level is actually enabled. In a hot transfer path at National Bank of India, building log strings that get thrown away is pure waste.

The Appender is an interface with implementations for console, file, and remote destinations, which is the Strategy pattern. Adding a new sink like a database or Kafka is a new class rather than a change to the Logger. The Formatter is pluggable the same way, so switching from plain text to structured JSON is a configuration choice.

Thread safety is non-negotiable because many transfer threads log at the same instant, and the log file must never get garbled. Synchronise appender writes for correctness, and in high-throughput services move to an asynchronous appender backed by a ring buffer so the business thread never blocks on I/O. The senior insight is that logging must be both cheap when disabled and safe under heavy concurrency, which is exactly why supplier lambdas and async appenders are essential.

Remember one sentence: a logging framework filters by level, formats through a pluggable formatter, fans out to strategy-based appenders, and must be both cheap when disabled and safe under concurrency.
